title: Resort Online Reputation Management: A Practical Guide
excerpt: How Indian resorts can manage reviews on Google, TripAdvisor, MakeMyTrip and Booking.com: asking every guest, replying well, handling unfair reviews and fixing what guests flag.
description: Resort online reputation management: ask every guest for reviews, reply well on Google and OTAs, handle unfair reviews, and fix recurring issues.
html:
Resort online reputation management means three habits: ask every guest for a review without filtering out unhappy ones, reply to reviews on Google, TripAdvisor, MakeMyTrip and Booking.com calmly and specifically, and use the themes in those reviews to fix how the resort runs. Disputing unfair reviews is a small part of the job.

Where resort reviews live and why each matters

Guests rarely read reviews in one place. They see your Google rating in search, read OTA reviews while comparing rooms, and some check TripAdvisor for detail. Each platform plays a slightly different role.

  • Google: shown in your business panel and on Maps, often the first rating a guest sees. You can reply to every review from your Business Profile.
  • MakeMyTrip, Goibibo, Booking.com and Agoda: reviews are tied to verified stays and appear right beside the "Book" button. They also feed into how the OTA presents your listing.
  • TripAdvisor: longer, more detailed reviews, often read by international guests and people planning longer trips.
  • Airbnb: two-way reviews between host and guest, important if you list villas or cottages there.

You do not need to be equally active everywhere. Prioritise where your bookings come from, plus Google, because almost every guest sees it.

Ask every guest, without gating

Review gating means asking guests how their stay was first, then only sending happy ones to Google or the OTA. It is tempting, and it is a bad idea. Google's review policies prohibit selectively soliciting positive reviews, and gating also hides the feedback you most need. Ask everyone the same way.

A simple routine that works for most resorts:

  1. At checkout, a staff member thanks the guest and says you would value a review. Keep it human, not scripted.
  2. Within a day, send a WhatsApp message with a direct link to your Google review form. One link, one sentence.
  3. For OTA guests, the platform usually sends its own review request. A short in-stay reminder is enough.
  4. Never offer a discount, free meal or gift in exchange for a review. Most platforms prohibit incentivised reviews.

Steady requests matter more than big pushes. A trickle of recent reviews every week reads as more trustworthy than fifty in one month and none for the next six.

How to reply to reviews

Your replies are read by future guests more than by the reviewer. Write for that audience.

Principles for every reply

  • Reply to all reviews, positive and negative, within a few days.
  • Use the guest's name if shown and mention something specific from their review.
  • Keep it short. Three or four sentences is usually enough.
  • Sign off with a real name and role, such as the general manager.
  • Do not copy-paste the same reply. Guests notice.
  • Never share booking details, phone numbers or anything private in a public reply.

Replying to a negative review

Thank the guest, acknowledge the specific problem without arguing, say what you have done or will do about it, and offer a way to continue the conversation privately. For example: "Thank you for telling us about the hot water in the hillside cottages, Priya. You are right that it took too long to arrive in the mornings. We have since added a booster to that block. I would like to hear more; please message me on our WhatsApp number." Calm, specific and short.

Avoid defensive replies that list everything the guest got wrong. Even when you are right, future guests mainly notice the tone.

Handling unfair or fake reviews

Some reviews are genuinely unfair: written by someone who never stayed, posted by a competitor, or containing abuse. Each platform has a process to report them.

  • On Google, you can flag a review from your Business Profile if it breaks Google's policies, such as fake engagement, off-topic content, or harassment.
  • On OTAs, use the extranet's review dispute or report option and provide booking details if the reviewer did not stay.
  • On TripAdvisor, use the management centre to report a review that breaks its guidelines.

A review being harsh or inaccurate in your view is usually not enough for removal. If a report is declined, write a factual, polite reply so other guests see your side. Do not threaten reviewers or ask them to delete reviews in exchange for refunds.

Use review themes to fix operations

This is where reputation management pays back. Once a month, read every review from the past month and tag each comment by theme. A simple table is enough.

Rooms and maintenanceMaintenance
Location and accessManager
Value for moneyOwner
Wi-Fi and powerMaintenance

Patterns emerge quickly. If several guests mention that the road to your Coorg property is hard to find at night, the fix is a better pin, signage and a directions message on WhatsApp before arrival, not a better reply. If Kerala guests keep praising a particular cook's breakfast, put that in your listing and photos.

Share the table with heads of department. Reviews are free, unprompted feedback from your actual guests, and they are often more useful than an internal survey.

Using reviews in your marketing

Good reviews can support your other channels, as long as you use them honestly.

  • Show your Google or OTA rating on your website with a link to the source, kept up to date.
  • Quote short, real excerpts on relevant pages, such as a review about the pool on your family package page, with the guest's first name and permission where the platform requires it.
  • Use recurring praise to guide your photos and content. If guests love the sunrise view, make sure it is the first image on your listing.

For how reviews fit into the bigger plan, see the resort digital marketing plan, and for how ratings affect what guests trust on your site, the post on resort photography and video shows how to keep images matched to reality. More on our approach is on the hospitality page.

Frequently asked questions

Should a resort reply to every review, including positive ones?

Yes, ideally. Replies to positive reviews show future guests that real people run the property and read what guests say. Keep them short and specific rather than generic thanks. For a small resort with a handful of reviews a week, this takes a few minutes. If volume is high, prioritise negative and detailed reviews, then work through the rest.

Is it allowed to ask only happy guests for reviews?

No. Google's policies prohibit selectively asking for positive reviews, and many OTAs have similar rules. Beyond the policy risk, filtering hides the feedback you most need to improve. Ask every guest the same way, at checkout and with a follow-up message, and let the reviews reflect the real experience. Then reply well to the ones that are critical.

Can I get a bad review removed from Google?

Only if it breaks Google's policies, for example if it is fake, off-topic, or contains harassment or hate speech. You can flag it from your Business Profile and request a review. A review that is simply negative or that you disagree with will usually stay. In that case, a calm, factual reply is the best way to put your side forward for future guests.

How often should we review guest feedback internally?

Monthly works well for most resorts. Read all reviews from the month, tag them by theme such as food, cleanliness, service and maintenance, and assign one action per recurring problem to a named person. Check the next month whether that theme has improved. Respond to individual reviews within a few days; do the theme analysis once a month.

Where to start

Create a direct Google review link from your Business Profile and add it to a short WhatsApp checkout message that every guest receives. Reply to any unanswered reviews from the last three months. At the end of the month, tag every review by theme using the table above and pick one fix.
